chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn Shira from Muhammad ibn Sulayman from al-Husayn al-Marjusi from Hisham, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'The people question us and refute our statement that no prayer is performed over a child because he has not prayed.' They say: 'Prayer is not performed except over one who has prayed.' So we say: 'Yes.' They ask: 'What do you think if a Christian or a Jew embraced Islam and then died immediately, what is the answer regarding him?' He said: 'Tell them: What do you think if this one who embraced Islam immediately then committed a false accusation (against someone), is it obligatory upon him regarding his false accusation?' They will say: 'It is obligatory upon him to receive the lash (hadd).' So when they say this, it is said to them: 'What if this child who has not prayed committed a false accusation against someone, is it obligatory upon him to receive the lash?' They will say: 'No.' Then it is said to them: 'You are correct. Prayer is only performed over one upon whom prayer and the lash are obligatory, and prayer is not performed over one upon whom prayer and the lashes are not obligatory.'
ai.seo_question: Why is funeral prayer performed over infants who have not yet prayed?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) employs a nuanced legal analogy (qiyas) to refute the objection that funeral prayer requires personal performance of prayer, arguing instead that it is linked to the obligation of legal penalties (hudud). By noting that an infant or immediate convert is exempt from lashes for false accusation due to lack of full legal capacity (bulugh), he establishes that the absence of personal prayer does not preclude the community from praying over them. This hadith is foundational in Shia jurisprudence for distinguishing between the ritual duty of the individual and the communal right of funeral prayer.
